candidates.title: Goal Engineering: How to Design Goals
candidates.author: Harrison Chase; Mihir Garimella and Anshul Gupta (Actively AI)
candidates.what_changed: Opinion/design essay arguing that for long-horizon, goal-driven agents, you should scope agents so that human feedback is as easy and high-quality as possible to give; 'Prompt engineering and context engineering will disappear, but goal engineering will remain.'
candidates.mechanism: Case study: Actively AI (sales agents) first built one agent per account (moving an account forward, proposing actions for reps to approve). Problems: reps context-switched across many agents with few items each, and learnings (how to outbound, how aggressive to be) were per-account but needed to transfer across accounts. V2 (built on LangChain Deep Agents) reorganizes agents into 'motions' - one agent per job-to-be-done (e.g., outbounding, early-stage deal progression) operating across many accounts; background context-gathering agents assemble per-account context that motions pull in as needed. Feedback on one task transfers to similar tasks in the same motion, and review is batched.
candidates.evidence_quality: Practitioner essay plus a qualitative customer case study; no metrics or evals reported. Co-authored by the customer; Deep Agents mention is a product plug.
candidates.relevance: high - concrete agent-decomposition pattern (scope agents by task type rather than by entity, so feedback aligns and transfers) plus 'invest in review UX'; directly actionable for teams building long-running agents.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: was UNVERIFIED (title only) in 2026-11-15 pass; extends LangChain's Nov 2 'New context engineering challenges in late 2026'
candidates.summary: Confirmed. Chase argues agent failures are mostly missing context, and the hardest context is tacit knowledge only humans hold, which arrives as feedback; so design the agent's scope to maximize ease and quality of feedback. Actively AI's re-architecture from per-account agents to per-'motion' agents (Deep Agents-based) is the worked example: batch-reviewable homogeneous tasks, learnings shared across accounts, objective account context gathered by separate background agents. Applied takeaways: decompose by job type rather than by customer/entity; separate objective context-gathering from judgment work; build a good review UX because feedback is the bottleneck. No quantitative results - treat as design guidance, not evidence.

candidates.title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
candidates.author: AWS (author names not extracted from page)
candidates.event_date: 2026-11-13 (AgentCore runtime platformVersion V2 and build hooks described as available; launch date of V2 not stated)
candidates.what_changed: AgentCore runtime V2 snapshots an initialized microVM once per create/update and restores it per session, so session start no longer grows with container image size; build hooks now supported.
candidates.mechanism: Snapshot/restore of microVM memory+disk (Lambda SnapStart-like); file cache cleared before freeze; image blocks lazily fetched on first read; two-phase warmup hook (memory before snapshot, disk after test restore).
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor engineering guidance with code and configuration; latency figures (~2 s new session, ~200 ms warm) are vendor-stated, no benchmark methodology or distributions published.
candidates.relevance: high - concrete agent-runtime ops engineering: cold start, snapshot pitfalls (shared RNG state, monotonic clocks, stale sockets/credentials) that generalize to any snapshot-based agent sandbox.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: none direct; adjacent to agent observability (uses CloudWatch Latency/OverheadLatency metrics) but distinct topic.; carried over from 2026-11-15 pass C.json (not re-read today)
candidates.summary: AWS describes how AgentCore runtime with platformVersion="V2" changes session startup. V1 pulled the container image from ECR per session, so cold start scaled with image size. V2, on each create/update, starts the container in a fresh microVM, waits for the first healthy GET /ping (must arrive within 120 s), clears the OS file cache, freezes the microVM, and stores memory and disk as a snapshot; each new session restores it, with process state (imports, objects, clients) intact and image blocks fetched lazily on first read. Trade-off: every create/update now takes a few minutes. Three stated consequences: memory (including /dev/shm) comes back whole; file reads during init do not carry over; image files are fetched on first read. Guidance inverts usual cold-start advice: do all static work before app.run() (imports, boto3 clients, objects, prompts/indexes held in memory, long-running helper processes like language servers), copy toolchains (e.g., tsc) to /dev/shm, ship compiled bytecode (UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1). Close non-boto3 network connections before the snapshot (stale sockets add hundreds of ms). New build hooks (hooksConfiguration.build.warmup, httpPost path/port 8000-12000) receive two POSTs distinguished by header X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Warmup-Type: 'memory' (pre-snapshot, state is captured) and 'disk' (after test restore, primes which files sessions fetch first); both share the 120 s budget, any non-2xx fails the deploy with no retry; UpdateAgentRuntime replaces the whole hook config. Snapshot pitfalls flagged as bugs or security issues: Python random/NumPy state created during init is identical in every session (generate nonces/keys in the handler with secrets/os.urandom/uuid4); init timestamps are frozen and time.monotonic() does not count stored time, so rate limiters/TTL caches must use wall clock; fetched credentials may be expired at restore; dynamic data (AgentCore Gateway tool catalogs, feature flags) should be loaded per session with an expiry (sessions last up to 8 h; idle timeout default 15 min, 60 s-8 h). Measurement: CloudWatch AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore Latency (TTFB) and OverheadLatency (platform part); report P90/P99 or TM90; init time appears only in build logs. Vendor claim: new session ~2 s, running session ~200 ms; for sub-second, pre-warm a session (session IDs need >=33 chars) when the user opens the chat, at the cost of sessions for users who never prompt. Quote: "for random values, a security issue."

candidates.title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
candidates.author: AWS (author names not extracted from page)
candidates.organization: AWS Machine Learning Blog (with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard)
candidates.what_changed: Sample CDK deployment of LiteLLM v1.102.0 with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard (switchyard-server 0.3.0) routing plugin on Bedrock plus benchmark runners that measure cost per solved task vs single-model baselines.
candidates.mechanism: Stage routing reads the last N tool results in request history and escalates from an efficient model (Nemotron 3 Super 120B) to a capable model (Claude Opus 5.5) on failure signals; no judge model call.
candidates.evidence_quality: Reproducible sample code and methodology; explicitly publishes NO results ('A few runs on two tasks... aren't enough to draw conclusions'). Switchyard 0.3.0 labelled demo/evaluation, experimental integration.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Post states LiteLLM also shipped a native Switchyard stage router; not independently checked.
candidates.relevance: high - strong evals/inference-cost methodology: cost per solved task, not per token; candid caveats on escalation replay cost and statistical testing.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: partial overlap with 'versioned model routing and pricing' - differentiator is the task-level cost metric and history-signal routing.; carried over from 2026-11-15 pass C.json (not re-read today)
candidates.summary: Argues coding agents should be judged on cost per solved task (total run cost / runs whose tests pass), since turns, replayed history, retries and failed attempts dominate cost. Switchyard is an open-source NVIDIA library; its LiteLLM integration supports Stage (exactly two candidates, capable listed first; reads tool activity/results in history; picker='efficient_first', confidence_threshold=0.5, recent_window=3) and Random (weighted, e.g. [0.5,0.5] for A/B). Classifier-backed Task/Composite routing unsupported because it needs intermediate model calls. A new request with no tool results goes to the efficient model. Architecture: LiteLLM+plugin in one container on ECS Fargate in private subnets, ALB path allowlist (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/models, /health/liveliness; everything else 404), WAF with 2,000 req/5 min per IP and generic XSS/SQLi body rules omitted because agent source code trips them, stack refuses 0.0.0.0/0 or IPv6 CIDRs, gateway key from Secrets Manager, Bedrock Converse via VPC endpoint; x-litellm-model-name header reveals which model answered. Models: global.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 and nvidia.nemotron-super-3-120b; warning that global cross-Region profiles may process data worldwide. Agent must send full history; Responses and Anthropic Messages paths not forwarded. Bench: bench/run.py tasks slugify, roman, calc, lru_ttl (6 turns default); unpriced turns (cached input, missing price) marked n/a rather than zero; bench/multiturn.py with per-conversation cost caps. Interpretation guidance: compare SOLVED before COST/SOLVED; Stage cannot pre-route hard tasks and an escalated turn replays the whole failed attempt, possibly costing more than starting on the capable model; use Fisher's exact test; max_tokens truncation makes cost a lower bound. Runners execute model-written code without an OS sandbox. Quote: "the number that matters is cost per solved task".

candidates.summary: Vendor-reported figures: 50+ framework families attempted to scan Cloudflare customers in the last three days; IPs running them in the thousands; daily requests from AI pentest/exploitation tools up 30x since Oct 1 and >10x since ARTEX's Oct 8 takedown by its creator (Autumn-27) - a 'hydra effect' producing 12,000+ repositories, several hundred unique forks (chart shows 204 public repos with code changes); ARTEX+forks are >60% of known orchestrators as of Nov 12. Table of top five (1k+ stars, fully autonomous): ARTEX (planner + parallel agents; goal/leads/findings graph linked to asset graph; runs on host/container with root, builds tools), LuaN1aoAgent (supervisor/planner/executors, three graphs, built-in SSH and Chisel tunneling with reconnection), Decepticon (orchestrator + specialist sub-agents, Kali root, AD/cloud pivot skills), Cairn (dispatcher to existing harnesses Codex, Claude Code, Pi; graph of facts and leads), PentestGPT-Agent. Argues autonomy makes compromise 'hill-climbable'. IR: multiple incidents where attackers got into a hyperscaler, then pivoted into the customer's Cloudflare account via static, non-expiring CI/CD tokens with no IP restriction; observed Worker scripts named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, artex-do-*, >69 requests/min across infrastructure, 400 database dump requests in an hour, persistence attempts and third-party session-token validation; activity believed lightly human-guided. Recommendations ('Modern Security Model', six pillars): WAF + rate limits, anomaly detection, bot defense, identity-gated access + micro-segmentation, OpenAPI schema validation + mTLS + default-deny, threat intel. candidates.title: Advancing science & engineering with Antigravity's /teamwork
candidates.author: Vahab Mirrokni (Google Fellow and VP, Google Research)
candidates.what_changed: Google reports results from /teamwork multi-agent harness patterns (with Gemini 4 Argon/Carbon/Hydrogen) and says /teamwork, /boost and Deep Review are available in Antigravity, with formal-proof and rewrite patterns coming.
candidates.mechanism: Parallel exploration paired with dedicated falsifiers (Lean 4, unmodified test suites, simulators, hardware counters); context partitioned per agent; coordinators hand off to fresh successors; critics/auditors verify from clean contexts; declarative self-improving natural-language patterns with prompt routing.
candidates.evidence_quality: Vendor claims across many results; some are machine-checked (Lean) or measured against test suites, but most details live in linked papers not read here. Survey N=70 for Deep Review.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Academic co-authors listed (CUHK, USC, CMU, Columbia, etc.); no independent replication checked.
candidates.relevance: high - multi-agent harness design (context partitioning, falsifier-based verification, dependency-ordered rewrites to stop agents gaming tests, proxy evaluators validated by rank correlation).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: touches multi-agent themes but not permission boundaries; no direct overlap.; carried over from 2026-11-15 pass C.json (not re-read today)
candidates.summary: Design rationale: generation is unpredictable, so pair parallel attempts with falsifiers; long tasks lose detail, so partition context by construction - each agent gets only needed files/tools, coordinators hand off to fresh successors, critics audit without producer reasoning. /boost packages a sequential solve-and-verify loop; a /teamwork campaign analyzing past trajectories found tightly coupled code is better handled sequentially than via parallel splits ('a harness optimizing another harness'). Vendor-reported results: Courtade-Kumar conjecture (2013) proved, formalized in Lean 4 at 50 million lines; /teamwork-LEAP autonomously formalized the Weil conjectures (~1.8M lines Lean, 28,800 subagent invocations) and Hilbert's tenth problem over rings of integers (>919,000 lines); NMR structure elucidation with 30 agents + spectral simulator: 95% top-1, 100% top-3, ~2x single-agent; causal-inference benchmark built by 29 agents in 11.5 h from 13 tables (50 tasks). Engineering: Zircon microkernel C++->Rust remainder (~800,000 lines safe Rust, passes kernel unit tests, boots on arm64) via a rewrite pattern that schedules modules only after dependencies compile and links leaves against the original unmodified test suite (to stop stubbing/test edits); libgav1 to ~170k lines Rust, bit-exact, initially ~4x slower then 20-30% faster than C++/assembly after profiling access; DuoDiscover builds 23-second proxy 'yardsticks' for 7-32 min TPU kernel evals, validated by Kendall rank correlation: 4.09x geomean over 17 JAXBench kernels, 2.99x over 7 vLLM TPU Pallas kernels; FarArray 60-90x throughput; Borg scheduling change: 24% less TPU preemption on some hardware; 9x9 Go engine +~2,600 Elo in <8 days. Deep Review: 578 STOC 2027 submissions opted in; survey N=70: 90% rated feedback mostly factual, >30% found substantive proof bugs. Access: 10,000 academic researchers get six months free top tier. Quote: "partitions context by construction".
